newsitem.title: ZAIRE: World fears calamity in Zaire as more flee warfare.
newsitem.headline: World fears calamity in Zaire as more flee warfare.

text.p: Ethnic warfare has pushed Zaire to the brink of calamity with about half a million people roaming the bush in search of safe havens, aid workers said.
As Africa's worst humanitarian disaster loomed in chaotic central African Zaire, European politicians called for action.
Aid workers said some 400,000 refugees had already packed Mugunga camp, near Goma. Half that number arrived in the last 24 hours.
"Another 200,000 refugees arrived in the camp in the last 24 hours...with close to half a million people in there," U.N. official Panos Moumtzis said on Monday night.

"This is now the largest refugee camp in the world," declared U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa in New York. "This is not good news because it is built on a volcanic rock and adding more latrines and water is a nightmare."
Foa said the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR now had access to only about 400,000 of the one million refugees in eastern Zaire.

"Right now there is about half a million people who are really running around, they haven't reached any camp and are not receiving any assistance from anybody," the UNHCR's Mountzis, told Cable News network from Goma.
U.S. charity American Refugee Committee, which says it has primary health care responsibility for Mugunga camp, estimates the refugee population there at about 400,000.
It said in a fax from its Minneapolis base that the camp had one foreign doctor, Michael Vjecha, who was assisted by 14 Rwandan doctors and 130 Rwandan nurses.

"The health status of these refugees is pretty good at the moment because they've been well cared for at nearby camps. But with a shortage of food, water and sanitation facilities we're on the brink of a public health disaster unless additional aid can be quickly provided," it said, quoting Vjecha.
Zaire hardened its tone in the conflict between its army and Banyamulenge Tutsis, who settled from Rwanda 200 years ago.
It paraded 10 alleged Rwandan army "prisoners of war" and state media urged the army to hit Rwanda hard.
The state television said the 10 were seized trying to sabotage the airport at Bukavu, the frontline of fighting between the army and ethnic Tutsis.

Zaire accuses Tutsi regimes in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi of helping the Banyamulenge Tutsis. Both Rwanda and Burundi deny involvement in the conflict which threatens to engulf the entire Great Lakes region of Central Africa.
Underlying the violence is the historic Hutu-Tutsi rivalry which exploded in the 1994 massacres of up to a million Tutsis in Rwanda by Hutus.
Most of the people fleeing eastern Zaire are Hutus who escaped the violence in Rwanda and are still afraid to return.
Ethnic rivalry in eastern Zaire degenerated into clashes with the arrival of more than a million Rwandan Hutu refugees in 1994. Hutus also fled violence in Burundi into the same region.
Minority Tutsi governments now in charge in both Rwanda and Burundi accuse Zaire of condoning armed attacks by armed Hutus sheltered in Zaire and of persecuting ethnic Tutsi Zireans.
European politicians and diplomats in Brussels said Zaire, whose leader Mobutu Sese Seko is in a Swiss clinic after cancer treatment, could be approaching a political "meltdown".

"The end of Zaire has been predicted many times so I would urge caution," said one European Union diplomat. "But the combination of factors this time round makes this potentially the most destabilising event Africa has ever seen."
